# Hash-pinned install set for the LiteLLM proxy in .github/workflows/litellm-gateway.yml.
#
# Direct requirements: litellm[proxy]==1.106.0 prisma==0.15.0
#   opentelemetry-api==1.45.1 opentelemetry-sdk==1.45.1
#   opentelemetry-exporter-otlp-proto-http==1.45.1
#   (prisma is LiteLLM's own pin for its proxy database client, and the
#   OpenTelemetry packages are what its "otel" callback imports. The [proxy]
#   extra pulls in neither: without prisma the proxy will not start with
#   virtual keys and teams, and without OpenTelemetry the callback logs a
#   non-blocking import error and exports nothing. The OpenTelemetry versions
#   are the ones the local end-to-end run used.)
#
# Installed into its OWN virtualenv in that job, never next to clawmetry:
# LiteLLM pins its own fastapi / pydantic / openai stack, and the job is about
# talking to LiteLLM over the wire, not importing it.
#
# Hash-locked because LiteLLM has had compromised releases on PyPI; an exact
# version without hashes would still trust whatever the index serves.
# `prisma generate` in the job downloads Prisma's engine binaries, which this
# file cannot pin.
#
# Installed with `pip install --no-deps --require-hashes`. This is a complete
# resolved closure, so --no-deps costs nothing and buys the one thing that kept
# breaking: pip no longer re-derives litellm's metadata and enforces its
# unconditional `==` pins against this lock. litellm 1.83.7 pinned
# aiohttp==3.13.5, click==8.1.8 and python-dotenv==1.0.1 unconditionally, and a
# Dependabot security bump to any of the three used to make the whole file
# unsatisfiable -- #6006 (aiohttp) did, and left the job red on main. The pins
# litellm declares under `extra == "proxy"` were never checked at all, because
# this file locks litellm without that extra; that is why the cryptography,
# PyJWT and mcp bumps went green while aiohttp did not.
#
# So a bump to any single line here is now installable on its own. What that
# does NOT do is make it correct: a package bumped past what litellm 1.84.0
# expects is running untested against it, and the end-to-end job below is what
# says whether that is fine. Read a red run as the answer, not as a flake.
#
# SECURITY FLOORS LAYERED ON TOP OF THE RESOLUTION. litellm pins several of
# these unconditionally and at versions that carry open advisories, so they
# cannot come out of `uv pip compile` at all -- asking for them as constraints
# makes the file unsatisfiable (litellm 1.84.0 pins polars==1.38.1, and
# requiring polars>=1.39.3 alongside it resolves to nothing). The install is
# `--no-deps --require-hashes`, so the file may legitimately carry a higher
# version than litellm declares; that is already how this file has carried
# cryptography against litellm's lower pin. Currently layered:
#
#   cryptography==50.0.2        mcp==2.3.0         PyJWT==2.15.1
#   azure-identity==1.26.0      polars==2.0.0      polars-runtime-32==2.0.0
#   python-multipart==0.0.32    RestrictedPython==8.5
#
# Re-apply these after ANY regeneration. A plain recompile silently drops them
# back to litellm's own pins, which is a net regression even when the litellm
# bump itself clears advisories -- measured: a bare recompile at 1.84.0 trades
# litellm's 14 advisories for 3 HIGH each in cryptography, mcp and PyJWT.
#
# A regeneration is not the only way to lose one. The list above is prose, but
# every entry is spelled `Name==Version` -- which is also what an automated
# dependency bump searches this file for, and the comment matches before the
# real pin does. So a bump can land having edited only this list: the PyJWT
# floor was raised to 2.15.0 here while the pin below stayed at 2.13.0, and its
# 12 advisories came back under a green checkmark. Editing a version in this
# block is therefore never the whole change -- the pin below it, with every
# sha256 the release publishes, is what actually installs.
#
# tests/test_litellm_layered_floors.py now compares the two halves on every PR,
# so that particular silence is over. Keep the block's `Name==Version` spelling;
# that guard reads it.
#
# starlette and fastapi are NOT layered floors. They are the opposite: the
# resolution catching up with the litellm pin. This block used to read that
# starlette was "deliberately NOT layered", pinned to 0.50.0 by fastapi
# 0.124.4 "which litellm pins in turn", and that clearing its advisories
# "needs a fastapi bump from litellm upstream, not an edit here". That was
# true when written and is now stale, so the reasoning is recorded here
# rather than left to be re-derived.
#
# The upstream bump has happened. litellm 1.88.6 declares, under the [proxy]
# extra this file resolves WITH, fastapi >=0.136.3,<1.0 and starlette
# >=1.0.1,<2.0. The old pins were therefore BELOW litellm's own declared
# floors, not held up at them -- the file was carrying a fastapi two dozen
# releases older than the one litellm asks for, and the starlette that
# fastapi dragged along with it. Re-running the documented `uv pip compile`
# on the direct requirements above resolves fastapi 0.142.2 and starlette
# 1.7.0. What makes starlette 1.x reachable at all is that fastapi dropped
# its starlette ceiling by 0.136.3 (`starlette>=0.46.0`, no upper bound);
# 0.124.4 capped it at <0.51.0, which is what the old note described.
#
# FASTAPI IS HELD AT 0.141.1, NOT THE 0.142.2 A FRESH COMPILE RESOLVES, AND
# THE REASON IS MEASURED, NOT PRECAUTIONARY. fastapi 0.142.0 added
# `opentelemetry-api>=1.44.0` as a CORE dependency -- fastapi instruments
# itself now -- and that collides with litellm's own OpenTelemetry callback,
# which this file installs on purpose (the otel packages are direct
# requirements above, for the proxy's "otel" callback). Taking 0.142.2 leaves
# the proxy serving traffic correctly, and the whole spend reconciliation in
# litellm-gateway.yml still passes, but TRACE CORRELATION breaks: the job's
# `correlated == 1` assertion fails, because litellm's spans are being ended
# underneath it.
#
# Measured on PR #6232 against the last green main run of the same job:
#
#                                   green main   fastapi 0.142.2
#   litellm _to_ns(None) failures            0                 5
#   "Calling end() on an ended span"         0                 3
#   gateway trace-correlation assertion   pass              FAIL
#
# The failures are litellm's `async_service_success_hook` ->
# `opentelemetry.py::_to_ns(start_time)` raising on a None start_time, plus
# span-lifecycle complaints; all of them appear only with 0.142.x. 0.141.1 is
# the newest fastapi with NO core opentelemetry dependency, satisfies
# litellm's `>=0.136.3`, carries no advisory of its own, and needs nothing
# the closure does not already pin (starlette>=0.46.0, pydantic>=2.9.0,
# typing-extensions>=4.8.0, typing-inspection>=0.4.2, annotated-doc>=0.0.2).
#
# So do not "finish the job" by moving fastapi to 0.142.x here. That is not a
# version lag; it is the boundary, and it moves when litellm's otel
# integration stops ending its own spans early under a self-instrumenting
# fastapi. The end-to-end job is what says so -- read a red correlation
# assertion as the answer, not a flake.
#
# Taken as a two-pin edit rather than a regeneration, because nothing else in
# the closure needs to move. Every other starlette/fastapi consumer here is
# already ceiling-free -- mcp 1.28.1 asks starlette>=0.27, sse-starlette
# 3.4.11 asks starlette>=0.49.1, fastapi-sso 0.19.0 asks fastapi>=0.80 -- and
# both new versions' own requirements are satisfied by what is already pinned
# below: fastapi 0.142.2 wants pydantic>=2.9.0, typing-extensions>=4.8.0,
# typing-inspection>=0.4.2, annotated-doc>=0.0.2 and
# opentelemetry-api>=1.44.0; starlette 1.7.0 wants anyio>=4.0.0,<5 and
# typing-extensions>=4.10.0. A full recompile was measured as well and would
# have moved 29 further packages and added numpy and granian to the closure;
# that is a different change with a different risk, and it is not needed to
# clear these advisories.
#
# Clears PYSEC-2026-2280, PYSEC-2026-2281, PYSEC-2026-248 and PYSEC-2026-249
# (pip-audit against this file reports no remaining advisory). These two are
# NOT added to the layered-floor block above: that block is for versions held
# ABOVE what litellm declares, and these two are versions litellm itself
# requires, so a future regeneration resolves them without hand re-application.
# The end-to-end job in litellm-gateway.yml is what says whether litellm 1.88.6
# is happy on the stack it asked for. Read a red run there as the answer.
#
# Regenerate: put the direct requirements above in ll.in, then
#   uv pip compile ll.in --generate-hashes --python-version 3.11 \
#     --python-platform x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu -o ci-litellm-proxy.txt
# then re-apply the security floors listed above.
